subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 16 periods = 640 minutes
Total: 16 periods · 10h 40min

periods.activity_title: Which unit fits? Matching lengths to metres and centimetres

tasks_in_class.description: Identify the appropriate units (m or cm) for: height of India Gate, handkerchief, well, mobile phone, elephant's trunk, shirt buttons.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Different Units but Same Measure, p.57
tasks_in_class.description: Find which measures (given in cm and m) represent the same sari or stole using the double number line.

time_bands.activity: Open with a quick class sort: hold up or name six everyday objects — India Gate, handkerchief, a well, a mobile phone, an elephant's trunk, shirt buttons — and ask children to call out whether they would measure each in metres or centimetres. Collect responses on the board without commenting on correctness yet.

Children work through Let Us Find, p.57 ("Identify the appropriate units (m or cm) for....") individually, writing their choices. Pairs then compare and justify disagreements — the teacher circulates, prompting: 'Would you hold a metre strip or a centimetre ruler to measure that?' Bring out the reasoning that very long or tall things need metres while small, hand-held things need centimetres.

Introduce the double number line from Different Units but Same Measure, p.57 ("Find which measures (given in cm and m) represent the same sari...."). Read the context aloud — Shikha and Sonu each measured the same cloth in different units. Children match measurements on the two scales, verbalising the connection: 100 cm sits below 1 m, 200 cm below 2 m. Discuss: 'Why do two different numbers describe the same length?' Close by establishing 100 cm = 1 m as the class's anchor fact.

periods.teacher_notes: A common error at this stage is treating metres and centimetres as interchangeable labels rather than as units with very different magnitudes — a child may write '5 m' for a mobile phone length. Pressing for a physical comparison ('Could you lay a metre stick beside it?') corrects this more durably than telling. The double number line's visual alignment of 100 cm and 1 m builds the multiplicative relationship that all later conversions depend on.

periods.activity_title: Walking a kilometre — steps, ropes, and the 1 000-metre idea

tasks_in_class.description: Measure 100 m and 200 m on playground with long tape; walk lines and count steps; use step-distance relationship to find distances of at least 3 locations; identify nearest and farthest from home; write distances in increasing order; name a location ≥1,000 m away.
Complete the table: for each rope length (100 m, 10 m, 200 m, 500 m, 250 m), find how many ropes are needed to make 1 km.

time_bands.activity: Ask the class: 'We measure cloth in metres. What unit would you use for the distance from school to your home?' Accept answers, then introduce the kilometre as the unit for long distances and write on the board: 1 km = 1 000 m. Briefly name the tools used to measure such distances — long tape, rodometer, rangefinder, laser distance meter — and show which one the class will use today.

Take the class to the playground for Let Us Do, p.59 ("Measure 100 m and 200 m on playground with long tape...."). In small groups children mark a 100 m line, walk it, and count steps. They record steps-per-100 m, then use that personal ratio to estimate the distances to at least three locations (school gate, water tap, main building). Back in a circle, groups share their nearest and farthest locations and arrange all distances in increasing order. Each group then names one place they know that is at least 1 000 m away.

Return to class and work on Let Us Explore, p.59 ("Complete the table: for each rope length…."). Children fill each row by asking: 'How many times does this rope length fit into 1 000 m?' — 100 m fits 10 times, 10 m fits 100 times, and so on. The teacher draws out the pattern: as the rope gets shorter, more are needed. Close by having children state the km definition in their own words.

periods.teacher_notes: Children often confuse the number of steps with the actual distance because step lengths vary; the key teaching move is to establish each child's personal step-to-metre ratio before using it for estimation. For the rope table, watch for the error of simply halving or doubling instead of dividing 1 000 by the rope length — press with 'How many 200 m ropes fit end-to-end into 1 000 m?' to surface the division structure.

section_titles: Kilometre race — applying km in context
periods.activity_title: Planning the race course — stations, marshals, and flags every set distance

tasks_in_class.description: Water stations every 500 m in a 3-km race — how many stations? At what positions from the start?
Children at 300 m intervals to direct runners in 3-km race — how many children needed? At what positions from the start?
Red and blue flags alternately every 50 m in a 3-km race — how many red and blue flags are needed till the finish line?

time_bands.activity: Draw a simple 3 km number line on the board, marked at 0 and 3 km, and ask: 'How long is this race in metres?' (Answer: 3 000 m.) Establish this conversion aloud before touching any question. Read the race scenario together and have children visualise: runners, water stations, marshals, flags — what does each question ask us to plan?

Pairs solve Let Us Do Q1, p.60 ("Water stations every 500 m in a 3-km race...."). Encourage marking positions on the number line drawn on the board — 500, 1 000, 1 500, 2 000, 2 500 m — and counting. One pair explains their answer; the class verifies by counting marks.

Children work individually on Let Us Do Q2, p.60 ("Children at 300 m intervals...."). Teacher circulates, asking 'Does a child stand at the start? At the finish?' to surface the boundary-counting nuance. Brief share-out; note the list of positions.

Groups of three tackle Let Us Do Q3, p.60 ("Red and blue flags alternately every 50 m...."). Children first find the total number of flags (3 000 ÷ 50 = 60 intervals, so 61 positions), then decide the red/blue split by the alternating pattern. Discuss: does the finish-line flag count? Close by comparing answers across groups and resolving any disagreement.

periods.teacher_notes: The most common error in all three questions is off-by-one counting — children often forget whether a placement occurs at the start, the finish, or both, leading to an answer that is one too few or one too many. Drawing the number line and physically marking each position is the most reliable corrective. For Q3, children may also confuse number of intervals (60) with number of placements (61); slowing down to count the first few positions by hand before generalising helps.

section_titles: Longest train journey — km arithmetic with data
periods.activity_title: Reading the Vivek Express table — computing totals, gaps, and comparisons

tasks_in_class.description: Find the total length of the route from Dibrugarh to Kanniyakumari.
Find the distance between Vijayawada and Jalpaiguri Road.
Which two stations are farther apart — Guwahati and Dimapur, or Bhubaneswar and Jalpaiguri Road?
Find the distance between Guwahati and Coimbatore JN.

homework.description: Find the distance between Vijayawada and Visakhapatnam.

time_bands.activity: Orient the class to the Vivek Express route: read the station names aloud in order from Dibrugarh to Kanniyakumari, and ask children to locate a few on a map sketch on the board (or in their textbook). Clarify how the table records cumulative distance from Dibrugarh so that the distance between any two stations is found by subtraction.

Children solve Longest Train Journey Q1, p.61 ("Find the total length of the route....") by reading the final entry in the distance column. Discuss why this works — because all distances are cumulative from one end. Then pairs work on Q2, p.61 ("Find the distance between Vijayawada and Jalpaiguri Road....") by identifying the two rows and subtracting.

Groups of three tackle Q4, p.61 ("Which two stations are farther apart — Guwahati and Dimapur, or Bhubaneswar and Jalpaiguri Road?"). Each group must compute both gaps, compare, and write a sentence explaining which pair is farther and by how much. Two groups share their reasoning; the class checks whether the numbers and conclusion agree.

Children work individually on Q5, p.61 ("Find the distance between Guwahati and Coimbatore JN."). Teacher circulates for calculation errors. A quick check: does the answer feel reasonable given that Q2's answer (Vijayawada to Jalpaiguri Road) spans a similar portion of the route? Children who finish early are encouraged to estimate the distance between two self-chosen stations and verify.

periods.teacher_notes: Children frequently subtract the smaller cumulative distance from the larger without identifying which station comes first on the route, leading to correct arithmetic but confused reasoning — press them to name both stations and say which is farther from Dibrugarh before subtracting. Q4 is a comparison question: the teaching move is to insist that both gaps must be computed before any judgment is made, resisting the urge to guess from the station names alone.

section_titles: The world of small things — millimetre
periods.activity_title: Zooming in — discovering millimetres on the ruler and in living things

tasks_in_class.description: Examine the scale markings between 1 cm and 2 cm; count mm marks; discover 1 cm = 10 mm.
Measure the lines in the geometric design and write their measurements in cm and mm.
Soak moong/chana seeds; over 4 days take one seed each day and measure sprout length in mm; record in table.

time_bands.activity: Each child holds their 30 cm ruler and follows along with Let Us Explore, p.61 ("Examine the scale markings between 1 cm and 2 cm...."). Ask: 'How many small marks can you count between the 1 and the 2?' Children count aloud: ten marks. The teacher draws the segment on the board at large scale and labels each small mark 1 mm. Arrive together at 1 cm = 10 mm. Children write this in their notebooks as a discovery, not a given rule.

Children measure the lines in the geometric design using Let Us Measure, p.61 ("Measure the lines in the geometric design...."). They record each result in both forms — for example, 3 cm 4 mm — aligning the ruler carefully at the start of each line. Pairs check each other's readings; the teacher addresses ruler-placement errors and rounding to the nearest mm.

Introduce the sprouting experiment from Let Us Do, p.62 ("Soak moong/chana seeds; over 4 days...."). Distribute pre-soaked seeds (soaked before this sitting) and damp cotton/paper. Each child or pair sets up their observation tray, measures today's sprout with a ruler to the nearest mm, and records it as Day 1 in the table in the textbook. Discuss: why is mm more useful than cm for a tiny sprout? Arrange for seeds to stay in the classroom window for daily observation.

periods.teacher_notes: Children often miscount the mm marks because they start counting at the centimetre mark itself rather than at the first small division; clarifying 'count the gaps, not the lines' prevents this. For the geometric design measurements, a common difficulty is aligning the ruler so the zero — not the ruler's edge — sits at the start of the line; model this once at the board before children begin.

periods.activity_title: Drawing exact lengths and filling the unit-hierarchy number lines

tasks_in_class.description: Draw lines of lengths 5 cm 5 mm, 3 cm 6 mm, 8 cm 3 mm, 36 mm, 67 mm in notebook using a scale.
Fill in the blanks in the cm↔mm double number line (1 cm/10 mm to 50 cm/__ mm).
Fill in the blanks in the m↔cm double number line (1 m/__ cm to 21 m/__ cm).
Fill in the blanks in the km↔m double number line (1 km/1,000 m to 82 km/__ m).

time_bands.activity: Write the three anchor relationships on the board in a chain: 10 mm = 1 cm, 100 cm = 1 m, 1 000 m = 1 km. Read them aloud together once. Ask: 'If I want to go from mm all the way to km, what do I multiply by each step?' Build the multiplication path on the board collaboratively.

Children open notebooks and work through Let Us Draw, p.62 ("Draw lines of lengths 5 cm 5 mm, 3 cm 6 mm, 8 cm 3 mm, 36 mm, 67 mm...."). For the mixed-unit lengths they must first convert to pure mm to locate the endpoint on the ruler (e.g., 5 cm 5 mm = 55 mm), then draw carefully. The teacher circulates, checking that zero-end alignment is correct and that the drawn length is labelled in both forms.

Children complete the three double number lines: Q1(a) mm↔cm ("Fill in the blanks in the cm↔mm double number line...."), Q1(b) m↔cm ("Fill in the blanks in the m↔cm double number line...."), and Q1(c) km↔m ("Fill in the blanks in the km↔m double number line....") from Let Us Do, p.63. After each line, one child reads out a pair of values and explains the multiplication that links them, building a rhythm of 'multiply by 10 / multiply by 100 / multiply by 1 000'.

periods.teacher_notes: Discovering that 1 cm = 10 mm through ruler examination in the millimetre unit grounds the chain: this unit builds directly on that concrete finding to extend it upward to metres and kilometres. A frequent error when drawing mixed-unit lengths is using the cm value alone as the endpoint — for 5 cm 5 mm, a child may draw to the 5 cm mark and stop; prompt with 'How many millimetres altogether?' to require the full conversion before drawing.

periods.activity_title: Converting across all four units — a full-range drill

tasks_in_class.description: Convert: 4 cm 5 mm to mm; 89 mm to cm mm; 234 cm to mm; 514 mm to cm mm; 6 m 34 cm to cm; 20 m 12 cm to cm; 397 m to cm; 5,792 cm to m cm; 9,108 cm to m cm; 34 km to m; 6,870 m to km m; 10,552 m to km m; 29 km 30 m to m; 32 km 359 m to m.

time_bands.activity: Run a quick oral warm-up: the teacher calls out a unit relationship ('1 cm = ? mm?', '1 m = ? cm?', '1 km = ? m?') and children respond in chorus. Then model one conversion in each direction on the board — 3 cm 7 mm → mm, and 85 mm → cm mm — writing out the multiplication and division steps explicitly.

Children work through Let Us Do Q2, p.63–64 ("Convert: 4 cm 5 mm to mm; 89 mm to cm mm; 234 cm to mm....") in their notebooks. The 14 parts are arranged in four natural groups by boundary (mm↔cm, cm↔m, m↔km, km↔m compound forms); children may work through the groups in order. The teacher circulates, watching for the reversal error (multiplying when they should divide), and asks children who have finished a group to explain one of their steps to a neighbour.

A short whole-class check: the teacher calls out four of the 14 answers (one from each group), children hold up notebooks, and discrepancies are resolved immediately. Close with the key pattern: converting to a smaller unit means multiplying; converting to a larger unit means dividing.

periods.teacher_notes: The 14-part drill is designed to cover every conversion direction across the four-unit hierarchy built in the double-number-line unit; the breadth of this drill is the rationale for giving it a full sitting. The most common systematic error is applying the same multiplier across all pairs (e.g., always multiplying by 10) — circulating early to catch this prevents it from being reinforced across all 14 parts. Encourage children who convert correctly to express the relationship as a general rule: 'To go from cm to mm, I multiply by 10.'

periods.activity_title: Ribbon, roads, and gondolas — adding and subtracting compound lengths

tasks_in_class.description: Rani has ribbon rolls of 3 m 75 cm and 2 m 25 cm. How much ribbon in total?
Bhopal to Sanchi is 48 km 700 m; Bhadbhada Ghat waterfall is 17 km 900 m from Bhopal. How far is Sanchi from the waterfall?
Gulmarg Gondola section 1 is 2 km 300 m and section 2 is 2 km 650 m. Find total distance covered.

time_bands.activity: Model the two strategies for adding compound lengths on the board using a made-up example (e.g., 2 m 60 cm + 1 m 80 cm): Strategy 1 — add like units separately then regroup (60 cm + 80 cm = 140 cm = 1 m 40 cm; total 3 m 40 cm + 1 m = 4 m 40 cm); Strategy 2 — convert all to cm first (260 + 180 = 440 cm = 4 m 40 cm). Show both column layouts side by side. Ask: which strategy suits you?

Pairs work on Let Us Do Q1, p.66 ("Rani has ribbon rolls of 3 m 75 cm and 2 m 25 cm...."). Point out that 75 cm + 25 cm = 100 cm = 1 m — a clean regrouping. Children use whichever strategy they chose and compare their working with their partner's; both routes should give 6 m.

Children solve Q2, p.66 ("Bhopal to Sanchi is 48 km 700 m; Bhadbhada Ghat waterfall is 17 km 900 m from Bhopal....") individually. This is a subtraction problem requiring borrowing: 700 m − 900 m requires taking 1 km and converting it to 1 000 m. Teacher circulates; ask: 'Can you subtract 900 m from 700 m directly?'

Groups of two complete Q3, p.66 ("Gulmarg Gondola section 1 is 2 km 300 m and section 2 is 2 km 650 m...."). Sum the two sections; 300 m + 650 m = 950 m — no regrouping needed here. One group shares both working and answer. Close by naming the regrouping threshold: when the smaller-unit sum reaches or exceeds the conversion factor, carry one to the larger unit.

periods.teacher_notes: Borrowing in km+m subtraction (Q2) is the hardest move in this unit: children who have worked with compound lengths are comfortable adding, but subtracting when the smaller-unit part of the minuend is less than the subtrahend's smaller-unit part requires conceptual borrowing of 1 km = 1 000 m. Insisting that children write the expanded form (e.g., 48 km 700 m → 47 km 1 700 m) before subtracting makes the borrowing visible. The clean sum in Q1 (75 + 25 = 100 cm = 1 m) is worth celebrating as a 'nice number' moment.

periods.activity_title: Comparing lengths across units — circling the bigger and finding the gap

tasks_in_class.description: Circle the bigger length and find the difference for 7 pairs: 11 mm vs 1 cm; 26 mm vs 2 cm; 20 cm vs 201 mm; 1,020 mm vs 1 m; 2 m vs 245 cm; 5,678 m vs 6 km; 6 km 1,480 m vs 7 km 479 m.

time_bands.activity: Open with a brief oral warm-up — the teacher puts a pair of mixed-unit lengths on the board (e.g., '15 mm vs 2 cm') and asks children to discuss with a neighbour which is bigger before calling out. Establish the routine: to compare, first convert both to the same unit, then decide. Do two examples together on the board, writing the conversion step explicitly.

Children work through Let Us Do Q4, p.66 ("Circle the bigger length and find the difference for 7 pairs....") in their notebooks. For each pair they write: (a) both lengths in the same unit, (b) circle the bigger, (c) subtract to find the difference. Pairs include cross-boundary comparisons — mm vs cm, mm vs m, m vs km, and compound km vs compound km — requiring different conversion steps. The teacher moves through the room pausing at Pair 7 (6 km 1 480 m vs 7 km 479 m) where simplifying 1 480 m to 1 km 480 m first makes comparison easier.

Whole-class check on three selected pairs chosen to represent different boundary types. For each, a child reads out their conversion and the difference; the class signals agreement or flags a discrepancy. Close with the generalisation: 'Before comparing any two lengths, bring them to the same unit — then subtract to find how far apart they are.'

periods.teacher_notes: Q4 is a reasoning task more than a computation task: the central skill is deciding which unit to convert to, not merely executing the arithmetic. Children who can add and subtract compound lengths fluently (from adding and subtracting in the previous unit) sometimes still struggle here because the decision is theirs to make without a worked example to follow. A useful prompt: 'Which unit makes both numbers easier to compare — the smaller one or the larger one?' For pair 7, children who do not first simplify 1 480 m into 1 km 480 m end up comparing 7 km 480 m with 7 km 479 m after combining — a good opportunity to discuss how simplification reduces error.

periods.activity_title: Cloth, thread, and roads — multiplying and dividing compound lengths

tasks_in_class.description: Shop sells cloth at ₹100 for 5 m. Use the double number line to find cost or length for various quantities up to ₹2,000.
Anita needs 1 m thread per 50 cm sari border. How much thread for 5 m sari? Thread costs ₹50 per metre — how much money needed?
Road 12 km 600 m long is completed in 6 equal days. How much road is laid each day?

time_bands.activity: Model multiplication of a compound length on the board: 1 m 80 cm × 3. Strategy — multiply each part separately: 1 m × 3 = 3 m, 80 cm × 3 = 240 cm = 2 m 40 cm; total 5 m 40 cm. Then model division: 4 m 80 cm ÷ 4. Convert to cm (480 cm) ÷ 4 = 120 cm = 1 m 20 cm. Establish both the 'operate on each part' and 'convert then operate' routes.

Small groups work on Let Us Do Q2, p.67 ("Shop sells cloth at ₹100 for 5 m...."). Children fill the double number line — reading off known values and using the ₹100 per 5 m ratio (₹20 per m) to find missing costs or lengths. Groups share one non-trivial entry and explain the proportional reasoning behind it.

Children work individually on Q3, p.67 ("Anita needs 1 m thread per 50 cm sari border...."). Step 1: how many 50 cm lengths in 5 m? (10.) Step 2: 10 m of thread needed. Step 3: 10 × ₹50 = ₹500. Teacher circulates; the most common stall is at Step 1 — prompt with 'How many 50 cm pieces fit into 1 m?'

Pairs solve Q4, p.67 ("Road 12 km 600 m long is completed in 6 equal days...."). Children convert 12 km 600 m to 12 600 m, divide by 6 (12 600 ÷ 6 = 2 100 m = 2 km 100 m), and express the answer in compound form. One pair presents; the class verifies by multiplying back: 2 km 100 m × 6 = 12 km 600 m.

periods.teacher_notes: The proportional double number line in Q2 builds on the same pictorial tool used for cm↔m equivalence earlier in the chapter — recognising this connection helps children see multiplication and division of lengths as extensions of conversion thinking rather than a new procedure. For Q4, children who attempt to divide km and m parts separately (12 ÷ 6 = 2 km, 600 ÷ 6 = 100 m) arrive at the correct answer coincidentally here; probe whether they understand why this works and whether it would still work if 12 were not divisible by 6.

periods.activity_title: Feet, inches, and estimation — connecting metric to everyday informal units

tasks_in_class.description: Look at ruler to find inches; find how many cm and mm equal 1 inch; note 1 inch = 2 cm 5 mm, 1 foot = 12 inches or 30 cm.
Estimate the height of the tallest building in your neighbourhood; height of the tallest tree; depth of a well or swimming pool — share reasoning and reference used.
Stand against wall, mark your height; measure distance floor-to-mark in feet and inches; find tallest student in class and their height in feet and inches.

time_bands.activity: Children examine their 30 cm rulers for Let Us Explore, p.68 ("Look at ruler to find inches; find how many cm and mm equal 1 inch...."). Ask: 'Do you see any marks besides centimetres?' Children locate the inch scale on the reverse or side of the ruler, count mm marks spanning one inch, and record: 1 inch = 2 cm 5 mm. Establish also that 1 foot = 12 inches and approximately 30 cm, and that these are units people often use when describing rooms, buildings, and their own height.

Groups of three discuss and complete Let Us Estimate Q1–Q3, p.68 ("Estimate the height of the tallest building in your neighbourhood...."). Each group must name a reference they will use — a single-storey house is about 3–4 m, an electric pole about 6–8 m — and use it to reason toward their estimate, not to guess. Groups share: 'We think the building is about ___ m because ___.' The class hears at least two different reference-and-reasoning chains per question.

Try This, p.69 ("Stand against wall, mark your height; measure distance floor-to-mark in feet and inches...."). Children take turns standing against the wall while a partner marks their height with chalk or a sticky note, then measures from the floor to the mark using the ruler, expressing the result in feet and inches (and noting the cm equivalent). The class finds the tallest student's height in feet and inches. Discuss: why do people in India often give heights in feet and inches rather than metres and centimetres?

periods.teacher_notes: Children are often surprised that their ruler has an inch scale — taking time with the inquiry into the ruler itself before announcing the equivalences is worth it, because the discovery mode embeds the fact more durably than a statement. For estimation, the most productive teaching move is pressing for a named reference and a chain of reasoning rather than accepting a bare number; a child who says 'about 12 m because it looks like three single-storey houses stacked up' understands estimation strategy, while one who says '12 m' without a reference does not.
materials: Chalk or sticky notes for wall marking

periods.activity_title: Operation-sign puzzle — reasoning with arithmetic structure

tasks_in_class.description: Put appropriate operation signs (+, –, ×, ÷) in a 4×4 grid such that each row, column, and 4×4 box does not repeat any sign.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the puzzle from Try This (puzzle), p.69 ("Put appropriate operation signs (+, –, ×, ÷) in a 4×4 grid...."). Draw the empty 4×4 grid on the board. Ask: 'How many cells? How many different signs do we have? So how many of each sign appears in the completed grid?' (16 cells ÷ 4 signs = 4 of each.) Establish the rule: each row, each column, and the full 4×4 grid contains exactly one of each sign.

Children work in pairs or small groups on the puzzle in their notebooks. Encourage a systematic approach: start by placing signs in rows where the most constraints are visible, then check columns. When a pair reaches a conflict they cannot resolve, ask them to explain which sign is in each row and column so far — verbalising constraints often reveals the error. Different pairs may find different valid arrangements; that is mathematically legitimate.

Two pairs share their completed grids on the board. The class checks both: read each row aloud, then each column, counting signs. If both are valid, discuss: 'Are these the same solution or different ones?' This opens a brief discussion of uniqueness versus multiple solutions — a gentle encounter with mathematical openness. Close by asking each child to write one sentence about their strategy.

periods.teacher_notes: This puzzle is a genuine reasoning task — there is no length arithmetic involved, but the logical constraint-satisfaction structure is exactly the kind of critical thinking the chapter's context of measurement and problem-solving supports. Children who try random placement quickly find conflicts; nudging them toward a constraint-first strategy ('Which row has the fewest free cells?') develops systematic reasoning. Multiple valid solutions are possible and should be welcomed rather than resolved to a single 'right' answer.

section_titles: Kilometre race — applying km in context
Longest train journey — km arithmetic with data
periods.activity_title: Consolidation — unit sense, km reasoning, and data problems revisited

time_bands.activity: Open with a brisk oral unit-choice quiz: the teacher names a quantity (height of a building, width of a finger nail, length of a cricket pitch, distance from city to city) and children call out the appropriate unit — mm, cm, m, or km. For each answer, ask a child to justify: 'Why not centimetres for the city distance?' This reactivates the unit-sense reasoning from choosing appropriate units and the double number line equivalence.

Pose two fresh consolidation problems on the board. Problem A (kilometre reasoning): 'A running track is 400 m long. Meera runs 3 full laps. How far has she run? Give your answer in km and m.' Problem B (race-planning type): 'Flag posts are placed every 250 m along a 2 km path. How many flag posts are there, and at what distances from the start?' Children work in pairs, drawing number lines where helpful. One pair presents each answer; the class checks.

Post a small data table on the board modelled on the Vivek Express context — three stations with cumulative distances from a starting point (made-up data, e.g., Station A: 0 km; Station B: 345 km; Station C: 812 km). Ask three questions: total route length, distance between B and C, and which gap (A-to-B or B-to-C) is longer and by how much. Children work individually, then pairs compare. Close by reviewing the subtraction-from-cumulative-distance strategy.

periods.teacher_notes: This consolidation unit draws on the conceptual work of choosing appropriate units, equivalence between cm and m, the km definition, race-interval planning, and distance-table arithmetic — all content the class has explored — and presents it in fresh problem contexts to check whether children can transfer their reasoning rather than just recall procedures. Watch for children who can identify the correct unit but cannot convert or compute with it; that gap — unit sense without procedural fluency — is the most common partial understanding at this stage.

section_titles: The world of small things — millimetre
periods.activity_title: Consolidation — mm measurements, unit conversions, and compound arithmetic

time_bands.activity: Quick recall warm-up: write 1 cm = ? mm, 1 m = ? cm, 1 km = ? m on the board and have children fill in silently, then check by chorus. Then write three mixed-unit lengths (e.g., 4 cm 7 mm, 350 cm, 5 km 200 m) and ask children to convert each to the smallest unit present — mm, cm, and m respectively. One child works each conversion on the board while the class watches.

Pose four conversion questions of the same types covered in the relationships unit but with fresh numbers: (a) 7 cm 3 mm → mm; (b) 156 mm → cm mm; (c) 8 m 45 cm → cm; (d) 4 350 m → km m. Children work individually; the teacher circulates and flags any child who consistently reverses multiply/divide. After individual work, pairs check each other and resolve differences by showing the multiplication or division step.

Two compound-length problems are placed on the board. Problem A (addition with regrouping): 'A fence has three sections of 2 m 80 cm, 1 m 65 cm, and 3 m 90 cm. What is the total fence length?' Problem B (subtraction with borrowing): 'A road is 5 km 200 m long. Workers have completed 2 km 750 m. How much is left?' Children work individually, choosing their preferred strategy (operate-on-parts or convert-first). Each child writes which strategy they used and why. A class share-out closes the unit.

periods.teacher_notes: The three-addend fence problem in the consolidation requires two successive regroupings — this is a step beyond the two-addend examples in the adding and subtracting lengths unit and reveals whether children understand regrouping as a general process or only as a fixed algorithm for two quantities. Subtraction with borrowing (Problem B) revisits the hardest move from that unit: children who still subtract the smaller number from the larger regardless of position need the explicit borrowing-as-conversion prompt ('Take 1 m from 5 km 200 m and convert it to cm').

periods.activity_title: Consolidation — multiplying and dividing lengths, feet and inches, estimation

time_bands.activity: Briefly revisit the two strategies for multiplying compound lengths: operate-on-each-part separately, and convert-then-multiply. Place one example on the board: '3 m 40 cm × 5.' Children work it both ways in their notebooks, then compare to confirm both give the same answer. The teacher also models the division inverse: '17 m 00 cm ÷ 5.' This reactivates the multiplying and dividing lengths procedures before the consolidation problems.

Children work on two fresh compound multiplication/division problems. Problem A: 'A school garden has 8 identical rectangular plots, each 4 m 25 cm long. What is the total length of all plots placed end to end?' Problem B: 'A roll of cloth 18 m 60 cm long is cut into 6 equal pieces. How long is each piece?' Children work individually, writing a full solution including the conversion back to compound form. Pairs compare and resolve differences.

Round off the unit with a brief estimation and informal-units revisit. The teacher puts three estimation challenges on the board (height of the school building; length of the school corridor; depth of the storage room) and children first estimate in metres, then translate their estimate into feet and inches using 1 foot ≈ 30 cm. Partners compare estimates and discuss: do their reference objects (a door, a desk) give similar or different starting points? Close by naming the three informal-to-metric relationships: 1 inch = 2 cm 5 mm, 1 foot = 12 inches, 1 foot ≈ 30 cm.

periods.teacher_notes: Problem B (division: 18 m 60 cm ÷ 6) is chosen because 18 is divisible by 6 (giving 3 m) and 60 cm is divisible by 6 (giving 10 cm), so the operate-on-parts strategy works cleanly — this is a good moment to ask whether the strategy would still work if the numbers were not so convenient, nudging children to recognise when convert-then-divide is safer. The estimation activity at the close ensures that feet and inches are not treated as an isolated curiosity but as a genuine tool children can apply alongside their metric understanding.

periods.activity_title: Far and Near — a whole-chapter journey from millimetres to kilometres

time_bands.activity: Draw the complete metric unit chain on the board — mm → cm → m → km — with the scaling factors between each step (×10, ×100, ×1 000). Ask children to call out a real object whose size is best described by each unit, drawing on the full range the chapter explored: a sprout, a sari, the school playground, a train journey. This oral recap spans the chapter's span from millimetres to kilometres and grounds the synthesis in named, familiar referents.

Pose a multi-unit planning problem that spans the entire hierarchy: 'The school is organising a Health Walk of 2 km 500 m. A flag is placed at the start, then every 500 m. Drinking water is available every 250 m. The finish-line ribbon is 1 m 20 cm wide and is made of two equal pieces. How many flags are placed? How many water stops? What is the length of each ribbon piece in cm and mm?' Children work in groups of three, assigning one sub-problem each and combining answers. Each group presents its working.

An estimation and conversion round: the teacher names four quantities in informal or mixed units — '5 feet 4 inches; 3 km 780 m; 125 mm; 2 m 50 cm' — and asks children to convert each to the unit that makes it easiest to picture, writing their answer and a one-sentence justification. Pairs compare and discuss choices. This draws together the informal-units content, the full conversion hierarchy, and the unit-sense reasoning that opened the chapter.

Close with a whole-class reflection on the chapter's central idea: the same physical length can be expressed in many units, and choosing the right unit makes a measurement easy to understand and work with. Each child writes two sentences in their notebook: one describing the unit they found most surprising or interesting in the chapter, and one giving an example of when they would choose that unit in real life. Three children share; the teacher draws the connection back to the mm–cm–m–km chain on the board.

periods.teacher_notes: The multi-unit planning problem is designed so that each sub-problem (flag intervals, water stop intervals, ribbon division) touches a different section of the chapter — km interval counting, conversion, and compound division — and no sub-problem can be solved by someone who has only studied part of the chapter. The estimation-and-conversion round deliberately includes informal units (feet and inches) alongside metric to ensure the chapter's closing section is fully integrated. Watch for children who can convert correctly but cannot explain which unit is 'better' for a given quantity — that explanation is the dissolution-test skill this chapter builds.

items.prompt: Priya walks from the school gate to the library and counts 240 steps. She found earlier that 100 of her steps cover 80 m. Using her step-distance relationship, write how far the library is from the gate. Give your answer in metres.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 192 m. (240 steps × 0.8 m per step = 192 m.)
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the personal step-to-metre ratio: multiply steps counted by the distance each step covers.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student use a number line to count groups of 100 steps; stretch: ask them to express the distance in km and m as well.

exercise.description: Measure 100 m and 200 m on playground with long tape; walk lines and count steps; use step-distance relationship to find distances of at least 3 locations; identify nearest and farthest from home; write distances in increasing order; name a location ≥1,000 m away.

items.section_title: The world of small things — millimetre
items.prompt: Manu places his ruler along a pencil and reads: the pencil starts at the 0 mark and ends exactly halfway between the 8 cm mark and the 9 cm mark, at the fifth small mm mark after 8 cm. Write the length of the pencil in cm and mm, and also in mm only.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 8 cm 5 mm; 85 mm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Read the centimetre mark where the object is nearest, then count the remaining mm marks past it; convert by multiplying cm by 10 and adding the extra mm.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student draw the ruler segment and mark 8 cm, then count 5 mm ticks one by one; stretch: ask them to measure two classroom objects and record both in cm+mm and in mm only.

exercise.description: Examine the scale markings between 1 cm and 2 cm; count mm marks; discover 1 cm = 10 mm.

items.section_title: The world of small things — millimetre
items.prompt: A student measures a short line in a design. The line starts at 0 and ends between the 4 cm and 5 cm marks, at the seventh small mm mark after 4 cm. What is the correct measurement?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 4 cm 7 mm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Read the nearest centimetre mark below the endpoint, then count the remaining mm marks to reach the endpoint.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has read only the centimetre value and placed it in the wrong column, treating 4 cm 7 mm as a number of centimetres.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has correctly identified 4 cm but then multiplied 7 mm by 10, confusing the mm-to-cm conversion direction.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has mistakenly multiplied the centimetre reading by 10, showing confusion between the cm and mm scales.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student use a ruler to physically locate the 4 cm mark and count the seven mm ticks aloud; stretch: ask them to give the same measurement in mm only (47 mm).

exercise.description: Measure the lines in the geometric design and write their measurements in cm and mm.

items.prompt: On a ruler, Riya counts the mm marks that fit inside one inch mark. She finds 25 small mm marks and a bit more. Her teacher tells her the exact value is 1 inch = 2 cm 5 mm. Write 1 inch in mm only, and write 1 foot in cm.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 1 inch = 25 mm; 1 foot = 30 cm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Convert 2 cm 5 mm to mm by multiplying 2 × 10 and adding 5 to get 25 mm; use the given fact that 1 foot = 30 cm.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student convert 2 cm to mm first (20 mm) and then add the 5 mm; stretch: ask how many mm are in 1 foot (300 mm).

exercise.description: Look at ruler to find inches; find how many cm and mm equal 1 inch; note 1 inch = 2 cm 5 mm, 1 foot = 12 inches or 30 cm.

items.prompt: Kavya stands against the wall and her partner marks her height. They measure the mark from the floor and find it is 4 feet 3 inches from the ground. Write Kavya's height in cm. (Use: 1 foot = 30 cm, 1 inch = 2 cm 5 mm.)

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 129 cm 15 mm, which simplifies to 130 cm 5 mm. Working: 4 feet = 4 × 30 = 120 cm; 3 inches = 3 × 2 cm 5 mm = 6 cm 15 mm = 7 cm 5 mm; total = 120 + 7 cm 5 mm = 127 cm 5 mm. Alternate check: 4 feet 3 inches = 51 inches; 51 × 25 mm = 1 275 mm = 127 cm 5 mm. Answer: 127 cm 5 mm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Convert feet to cm (multiply by 30) and inches to cm+mm (multiply by 2 cm 5 mm), then add the two results.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: break it into two steps — first find 4 feet in cm, then 3 inches in cm, then add; stretch: ask the student to express the answer in mm only (1 275 mm).

exercise.description: Stand against wall, mark your height; measure distance floor-to-mark in feet and inches; find tallest student in class and their height in feet and inches.

items.prompt: Which unit is most appropriate to measure the length of a classroom blackboard?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Metres.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: A blackboard is several times the length of a 30 cm ruler, making metres the convenient and sensible unit — neither too large (km) nor too small (mm or cm).

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has chosen the smallest unit, suggesting they have not yet developed a sense of the magnitude that metres and centimetres represent.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student recognises cm as a length unit but has not yet applied magnitude reasoning — a blackboard in centimetres would be an awkward three-digit number.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student is confusing very long distances with everyday large objects, showing that the km boundary has not been internalised.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to hold a 30 cm ruler beside an imaginary blackboard and count how many rulers would be needed; stretch: ask them to estimate the blackboard length in metres and convert it to cm.

exercise.description: Identify the appropriate units (m or cm) for: height of India Gate, handkerchief, well, mobile phone, elephant's trunk, shirt buttons.

items.prompt: A dupatta is 250 cm long. Which of the following shows the same length in metres?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 2 m 50 cm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide the cm total by 100 to find the metres part (250 ÷ 100 = 2 m remainder 50 cm).

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has divided by 10 instead of 100, showing confusion about the cm-to-m conversion factor.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has correctly found 2 m but has mis-read the remainder as 5 cm instead of 50 cm — a place-value error.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has not applied the conversion at all and has only shifted a decimal place incorrectly.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student locate 250 on a cm↔m double number line and read across; stretch: ask them to also express the length in mm.

exercise.book_ref: Different Units but Same Measure, p.57
exercise.description: Find which measures (given in cm and m) represent the same sari or stole using the double number line.

items.prompt: A rope is 200 m long. How many of these ropes placed end to end are needed to make exactly 1 km? Explain how you found your answer.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide 1 000 m (the km definition) by the rope length to find how many fit end to end.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: encourage the student to draw a 1 000 m number line and mark off 200 m at a time, counting the marks; stretch: ask what fraction of 1 km one rope represents.

exercise.description: Complete the table: for each rope length (100 m, 10 m, 200 m, 500 m, 250 m), find how many ropes are needed to make 1 km.

items.section_title: Longest train journey — km arithmetic with data
items.prompt: The table below shows cumulative distances from Station P on a train route.
items.visual_stimulus:
Station | Distance from P
P | 0 km
Q | 310 km
R | 540 km
S | 780 km

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Q to R: 540 − 310 = 230 km. R to S: 780 − 540 = 240 km. R to S is farther apart, by 10 km.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Subtract the cumulative distance of the first station from the cumulative distance of the second station to find each gap; then compare the two gaps.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student first write the gap for Q-to-R before attempting R-to-S; stretch: ask them to find which two adjacent stations on the table are closest together.

exercise.description: Which two stations are farther apart — Guwahati and Dimapur, or Bhubaneswar and Jalpaiguri Road?

items.prompt: Which of the following lengths is the greatest?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 115 cm. Converting all to cm: A = 105 cm; B = 115 cm; C = 105 cm; D — dm is not in this chapter's scope, so if taken as 10 × 10 cm + 5 cm = 105 cm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Convert each length to centimetres and compare the resulting numbers.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has not converted correctly — 1 m 5 cm is 105 cm, not 115 cm.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student may have confused 1 050 mm with 115 cm; 1 050 mm = 105 cm, which is smaller than 115 cm.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may be guessing or has misread the compound unit; the value is equivalent to 105 cm.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student convert each option to cm one at a time before comparing; stretch: ask the student to rank all four lengths in order from smallest to largest.

exercise.description: Circle the bigger length and find the difference for 7 pairs: 11 mm vs 1 cm; 26 mm vs 2 cm; 20 cm vs 201 mm; 1,020 mm vs 1 m; 2 m vs 245 cm; 5,678 m vs 6 km; 6 km 1,480 m vs 7 km 479 m.

items.prompt: A shop sells rope at ₹80 for every 4 m. How much will 10 m of rope cost? Use a double number line or table to show your working.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Find the cost per metre by dividing ₹80 by 4, then multiply by the required length.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: help the student fill in ₹ for 2 m and 6 m on the number line first; stretch: ask how many metres can be bought for ₹500.

exercise.description: Shop sells cloth at ₹100 for 5 m. Use the double number line to find cost or length for various quantities up to ₹2,000.

items.prompt: Reena wants to estimate the height of the school flagpole. She knows that a single-storey classroom building near it is about 4 m tall. The flagpole looks roughly twice as tall as the building. Write Reena's estimate of the flagpole height in metres, and explain her reasoning.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: About 8 m. Reena used the building height (4 m) as a reference and doubled it because the flagpole looks about twice as tall.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Choose a known reference height and use visual comparison to scale it up or down to the unknown height.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to name only the reference and the comparison ('it looks twice as tall'); stretch: ask them to express the estimate in feet as well, using 1 foot ≈ 30 cm.

exercise.description: Estimate the height of the tallest building in your neighbourhood; height of the tallest tree; depth of a well or swimming pool — share reasoning and reference used.

items.prompt: In an operation-sign grid, the four signs +, −, ×, ÷ must each appear exactly once in every row and every column. The first row is already filled: +, −, ×, ÷ (from left to right). The first column has + in row 1. Which sign must go in the first column of row 2? Explain why.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The first column already has +. The four signs +, −, ×, ÷ must each appear once per column. So the first column of row 2 can be any of −, ×, or ÷ — not +. One valid answer is − (or × or ÷); the student must state that + is excluded because it is already used in column 1.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Check which signs are already used in the column and exclude them; any remaining sign is a valid choice.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw the partial grid with only the first row filled and ask the student to cross out the sign that cannot repeat; stretch: ask them to complete the entire first column consistently.

exercise.description: Put appropriate operation signs (+, –, ×, ÷) in a 4×4 grid such that each row, column, and 4×4 box does not repeat any sign.

items.prompt: What is 6 cm 4 mm expressed in millimetres only?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 64 mm.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply the cm part by 10 to convert to mm (6 × 10 = 60), then add the mm part (60 + 4 = 64 mm).

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has placed a zero between the cm and mm digits instead of multiplying — a place-value confusion.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has multiplied 6 by 100 instead of 10, applying the cm-to-m conversion factor instead of the mm-to-cm one.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has reversed the digits of the cm and mm values, indicating the conversion process is not understood.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student write 6 cm = ? mm first (60 mm), then add the 4 mm; stretch: ask them to convert 64 mm back to cm mm to verify.

exercise.description: Draw lines of lengths 5 cm 5 mm, 3 cm 6 mm, 8 cm 3 mm, 36 mm, 67 mm in notebook using a scale.

items.prompt: Convert 7 km 450 m into metres.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply the km part by 1 000 (7 × 1 000 = 7 000) and add the m part (7 000 + 450 = 7 450 m).
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student first write 7 km = 7 000 m separately, then add 450 m; stretch: ask them to also convert 7 450 m back to km m to verify.

exercise.description: Convert: 4 cm 5 mm to mm; 89 mm to cm mm; 234 cm to mm; 514 mm to cm mm; 6 m 34 cm to cm; 20 m 12 cm to cm; 397 m to cm; 5,792 cm to m cm; 9,108 cm to m cm; 34 km to m; 6,870 m to km m; 10,552 m to km m; 29 km 30 m to m; 32 km 359 m to m.

items.section_title: Kilometre race — applying km in context
items.prompt: A walking trail is 2 km long. Rest benches are placed every 400 m, starting from 400 m from the start. How many rest benches are placed along the trail before the finish line?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 4 benches. 2 km = 2 000 m; positions: 400 m, 800 m, 1 200 m, 1 600 m (the next would be 2 000 m = finish, so it is not 'before' the finish). 4 benches.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Convert the total distance to metres, divide by the interval to find the number of intervals, then count positions that fall before the finish.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw a number line from 0 to 2 000 m and mark each 400 m step; stretch: ask at what distances benches would be placed if the interval were 300 m instead.

exercise.description: Water stations every 500 m in a 3-km race — how many stations? At what positions from the start?

items.section_title: Kilometre race — applying km in context
items.prompt: In a 2 km fun run, yellow and green flags are placed alternately every 200 m, starting with a yellow flag at 200 m. How many yellow flags and how many green flags are there up to and including the finish line at 2 km?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Positions (m): 200 (yellow), 400 (green), 600 (yellow), 800 (green), 1 000 (yellow), 1 200 (green), 1 400 (yellow), 1 600 (green), 1 800 (yellow), 2 000 (green). Yellow: 5 flags. Green: 5 flags.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: List all flag positions by repeated addition of 200 m from 200 m to 2 000 m, assign colours alternately starting with yellow, then count each colour.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student list only the first four positions and their colours before continuing; stretch: ask what the colour of the flag at 2 500 m would be if the run were extended.

exercise.description: Red and blue flags alternately every 50 m in a 3-km race — how many red and blue flags are needed till the finish line?

items.section_title: Longest train journey — km arithmetic with data
items.prompt: A train route has four stops. The distances from the first stop are: Stop A — 0 km, Stop B — 218 km, Stop C — 465 km, Stop D — 712 km. What is the total length of the route from Stop A to Stop D?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 712 km. The total route length is the cumulative distance of the last stop from the first stop, which is given directly as 712 km.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Read the cumulative distance of the final stop; since all distances are measured from Stop A, that value is the total route length.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to first write what 'cumulative distance from Stop A' means; stretch: ask how far Stop B is from Stop C.

exercise.description: Find the total length of the route from Dibrugarh to Kanniyakumari.

items.prompt: A garden path has two sections. The first section is 3 km 600 m long and the second section is 1 km 750 m long. What is the total length of the path in km and m?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 5 km 350 m. Add km: 3 + 1 = 4 km. Add m: 600 + 750 = 1 350 m = 1 km 350 m. Total: 4 km + 1 km 350 m = 5 km 350 m.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add the km parts and the m parts separately; regroup when the m total reaches or exceeds 1 000 m.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student convert both lengths to metres first (3 600 + 1 750 = 5 350 m), then convert the total back; stretch: ask how much longer the path would need to be to reach exactly 6 km.

exercise.description: Bhopal to Sanchi is 48 km 700 m; Bhadbhada Ghat waterfall is 17 km 900 m from Bhopal. How far is Sanchi from the waterfall?

items.prompt: A cable car ride has two stages. Stage 1 is 1 km 800 m and Stage 2 is 2 km 450 m. What is the total distance of both stages together?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 4 km 250 m. Add km: 1 + 2 = 3 km. Add m: 800 + 450 = 1 250 m = 1 km 250 m. Total: 3 km + 1 km 250 m = 4 km 250 m.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add like-unit parts separately and regroup the metres total when it exceeds 1 000 m.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: convert to metres first (1 800 + 2 450 = 4 250 m) and then express in km m; stretch: ask how much farther Stage 2 is than Stage 1.

exercise.description: Gulmarg Gondola section 1 is 2 km 300 m and section 2 is 2 km 650 m. Find total distance covered.

items.prompt: Neha needs 1 m of ribbon for every 40 cm of box she decorates. She is decorating a box whose perimeter is 3 m 20 cm. How many metres of ribbon does she need? If ribbon costs ₹30 per metre, how much will she spend?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 3 m 20 cm = 320 cm. Number of 40 cm lengths in 320 cm: 320 ÷ 40 = 8. So Neha needs 8 m of ribbon. Cost: 8 × ₹30 = ₹240.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Convert the total length to cm, divide by the given interval (40 cm) to find the number of ribbon metres needed, then multiply by the cost per metre.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student first find how many 40 cm pieces fit into 1 m (2.5) or directly into 320 cm by listing multiples of 40; stretch: ask what happens to the cost if the perimeter increases by another 40 cm.

exercise.description: Anita needs 1 m thread per 50 cm sari border. How much thread for 5 m sari? Thread costs ₹50 per metre — how much money needed?

items.prompt: Workers are building a boundary wall 9 km 600 m long. They complete an equal portion every day for 8 days. How much wall do they build each day? Give your answer in km and m.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 1 km 200 m per day. 9 km 600 m = 9 600 m. 9 600 ÷ 8 = 1 200 m = 1 km 200 m. Verification: 1 200 m × 8 = 9 600 m = 9 km 600 m. ✓
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Convert the total length to metres, divide by the number of days, then express the quotient in km and m.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student convert 9 km 600 m to metres before dividing; stretch: ask how long it would take to build 15 km at the same daily rate.

exercise.description: Road 12 km 600 m long is completed in 6 equal days. How much road is laid each day?
